The Ħal-Saflieni Hypogeum actually relates to my work, fascinating thing. I'm researching Neolithic belief structures and spiritual ritualism in relation to the development of brain lateralization in the late Pleistocene. One of the things you come across near constantly is Megalithic structures with carefully designed psycho-acoustic properties - Gavrinis, Delphi, many Mesoamerican sites, Ħal-Saflieni - the acoustic phenomena pop up so damn frequently that there's now a dedicated field for their study, archaeoacoustics.

One working theory is that the sites were used to elicit psychedelic stimuli: unlateralized humans (whose brains worked as two distinct entities rather than one unified whole) may have been highly susceptible to auditory hallucinations (e.g. hearing voices and chants, not unlike schizophrenics) and they may have actively exploited psycho-acoustic phenomena to induce hallucinations of ancestral spirits and other spiritual entities. As lateralization progresses over time we're seeing more and more evidence of psychedelic drug use, which implies that people started using them to "offset" the fact that their ancestors slowly stopped communicating with them. Also interesting to note is that the Oracles of later time periods usually were women - who, even today, have significantly less lateralized hemispheres and may have been more sensible to the type of perception the job required.

For more on the topic I highly recommend Paul Devereux' work and everything Julian Jaynes has written on hallucinatory hearing. Deep rabbit hole to delve into, but extremely interesting.

Damn, glad I visited Voat this evening. Wasn't aware of this passage from Srimad Bhagavatam and it is indeed very interesting. I can't read Sanskrit yet, so I looked at this translation. Immediate eyebrow-raisers from 11.31.1 onward.

The forefathers, the perfected souls and divine singers, the scientists and the champions, the venerable ones, the treasure keepers and the wild men, the ones of superpower and the dancing girls of heaven and all the ones of Garuda, desirous to witness the passing away of the Supreme Lord, eagerly chanted and praised the birth and activities of Lord S'auri. Crowding the sky in a great number of vimânas oh King, they being joined in transcendental devotion showered flowers.

[...]

And while in heaven kettledrums resounded and flowers fell from the sky, Truth, Righteousness, Constancy, Fame and Beauty followed Him as He left the earth. [...]
Oh King, understand the appearance and the disappearance of the Supreme One among the embodied beings, to be a false show like that of an actor, enacted by His illusory potency. Creating this universe by Himself, entering it, engaging in pastimes in it and in the end winding it up, He ceases [with these functions] and remains in the greatness of the Supreme Self.

[Dâruka] told the story of the complete destruction of the Vrishnis oh ruler of man. When the people heard it they, with their hearts upset, were rendered senseless in their grief. Overwhelmed by the separation from Krishna, they struck their faces and quickly went to the place where their relatives were lying lifeless.

[...]

Arjuna saw to it that for the relatives who had died and who had no remaining family members, the funeral rites were executed in order of the seniority of the deceased as is prescribed.

I'm not well-read on this text and haven't cross-checked shit, so consider this low-effort spitballing:

  • the first passage strongly resembles sealing rituals that are speculated to have happened at other sites; the spiritual classes and tribes gather at a ritual site to witness a "passing" - a symbolic funeral rite maybe, which would be consistent with findings from Gavrinis and others?

  • Vimânas are those "heavenly vehicles" that are often interpreted as aircraft, right? Call it confirmation bias, but I believe it could actually make sense to link them to psychedelic drugs or psychedelic experiences in general. The text gives the definition of "divine palaces, different points of view or heavenly vehicles". Even a superficial understanding of Eastern philosophy tells you that a "divine palace" is a state of consciousness, not a literal location. Are "heavenly vehicles" a metaphor for something - a drug or a ritual - you use to reach those "divine palaces"?

  • "They being joined in transcendental devotion showered flowers" may be read as the description of a shared hallucination as part of a ritual, which may have included psychedelic drug use for some or all of the participants

  • "Truth, Righteousness, Constancy, Fame and Beauty followed Him as He left the earth" - this may be read as the description of the loss of the psychedelic qualities of unlateralized consciousness. Consistent with observations of a "sense of deeper meaning" and the loss thereof during and after psychedelic experiences and paranoid/schizophrenic episodes, and consistent with subjective reports of Amphetamine users (-> MDMA comedowns)

  • The entire paragraph on the appearance/disappearance of the Supreme One gives me a rock-hard scholar boner. I know that linking Vedic texts to consciousness research is damn thin ice that has ruined many reputations, but I think I'll risk having a look at this one from an evolutionary Neuroscience perspective one day

  • What do the people do when they hear of the "passing"? They quickly go the place where they keep their dead to execute funeral rites. And they make damn sure that no one is missed. Could this be compared to a final death rite, to lay all the ancestral spirits to rest? To make sure that no spirit is "trapped" in the now spirit-less world?

  • This would be consistent with Devereux' description of sealing ceremonies in Megalithic sites across Brittany, and it even coincides temporally; Bhagavatam roughly spans 8000 B.C. -2000 B.C., with the final Canto mostly concerning ~3100 B.C. - ritual passage graves started to appear elsewhere from 4250 B.C. - 3750 B.C. and our best guesstimate of when Gavrinis was sealed is 3340 B.C. - 2910 B.C.
